t: A royal letter, and different verse numbers
p: Chapter 4 opens as a letter from the king; the Aramaic verse numbers differ from the English.
b: Daniel 4 is a royal letter. The king greets his whole empire (4:1–3), tells his story in the first person (4:4–18), has Daniel's part told in the third person (4:19–33), and returns to the first person to close with praise (4:34–37). In the Hebrew Bible, what the English calls 4:1–3 is the end of chapter 3 (Aramaic 3:31–33), and English 4:4–37 is Aramaic 4:1–34. This site uses the English numbers everywhere. Nebuchadnezzar II ruled Babylon from 605 to 562 BC. The Old Greek, as Swete prints it, has no greeting at all (see the variant).

p: A standard Aramaic letter greeting, also used by Darius in 6:25.
orig: שְׁלָמְכוֹן יִשְׂגֵּא (shelamekhon yisgé), 'may your peace increase'
b: The Aramaic formula is shelamekhon yisgé, 'may your peace be great'. It is how royal letters open in the Aramaic parts of Ezra, where Persian officials write to the king and the king writes back. Using it here and in 6:25 makes Nebuchadnezzar's confession and Darius's decree read as official documents of the empire. Daniel 4 and Daniel 6 are the royal letters in the Bible that tell of a humbling or a rescue by Israel's God; the Persian kings' letters in Ezra (1:2-4; 7:12-26) also name him, but tell no such story.

t: Israel's words in a pagan king's mouth
p: 'Signs and wonders' is the language of the exodus, spoken here by the king who destroyed Jerusalem.
b: In Hebrew the pair otot umofetim describes what the LORD did to Egypt for Israel (Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 135:9). The Aramaic here, atayya utemahayya, is the same pair. The author lets Nebuchadnezzar, the conqueror of Jerusalem, speak the exodus vocabulary about what God did to him. Darius says it again in 6:27. The Plain keeps the pair the same in all three places. Whether the author means a real confession or a storyteller's pattern (a foreign king ends by praising Israel's God, as in 2:47 and 3:28–29) is one of the questions the chapter page weighs.

t: The song of an everlasting kingdom
p: These lines come back in 4:34, 6:26 and 7:14, 27, and are the theme of the whole book.
r: Daniel 2:44; Daniel 4:34; Daniel 6:26; Daniel 7:14; Daniel 7:27; Psalm 145:13; 2 Samuel 7:13, 16
b: Verse 3 is a short hymn: the signs and wonders show a kingdom that does not end. The Aramaic line 'his kingdom is a kingdom of alam' returns word for word in 4:34, and similar words close Darius's decree (6:26) and describe the one like a son of man (7:14) and the holy ones (7:27). The Plain keeps the same English in 4:3 and 4:34. Psalm 145:13 has nearly the same line in Hebrew. The book sets the passing kingdoms of Babylon, Media and Persia against this one that does not pass.

t: 'Green', a word that points to the tree
p: The Aramaic word for 'thriving' means 'green', the same picture as the tree of his dream.
b: Ra'anan is used of leafy, healthy trees (Psalm 92:14: the righteous are 'fresh and green' in old age; Jeremiah 17:8). The king describes himself with the picture that the dream will use against him. Most English versions say 'flourishing' or 'prospering' and lose the link. The word shelah, 'at ease', marks self-satisfaction here (Psalm 73:12 describes the carefree wicked with a different Hebrew word, shalev), and the chapter shows how quickly the king's ease ends.

t: The four kinds of wise men
p: Four classes of Babylonian experts fail again, as in chapter 2.
orig: חַרְטֻמַּיָּא אָשְׁפַיָּא כַּשְׂדָּאֵי גָּזְרַיָּא (chartummayya, ashshafayya, kasdai, gazrayya)
b: The list names learned men of the court. Chartummin ('magicians') is an Egyptian-origin word, used of Pharaoh's experts (Genesis 41:8; Exodus 7:11). Ashshafin ('enchanters') are specialists in spells. Kasdai ('Chaldeans') here means a learned class that studied the heavens and omens, not the people (compare 2:2, 10). Gazrin ('diviners', literally those who determine or cut out fates) read signs to say what had been decreed. The Plain gives each Aramaic word one English word through chapters 4 and 5 (the list in 5:7 and 5:11 repeats it).

p: The name Belteshazzar probably means 'protect his life', and the king connects it with his god Bel.
b: Daniel 1:7 says the chief of the eunuchs gave Daniel this name. Most scholars explain it as an Akkadian name of the type 'Bel, protect his life' (Balat-su-usur, with the god's name shortened), which fits the king's remark here that it matches 'the name of my god', Bel (Marduk, the patron god of Babylon; Isaiah 46:1; Jeremiah 50:2). The exact spelling is debated, and no one has found a Babylonian record of a court official with this name. The Plain spells it 'Belteshazzar', as in chapters 1 and 2.

a: a spirit of the holy gods
p: The Aramaic plural can mean 'the holy gods' or 'a holy God'; the Plain uses the king's pagan idiom.
b: Elahin is the plural of 'god', and in the mouth of a pagan king it means 'gods'. But Aramaic and Hebrew plurals (Elohim) can also mean the one God. The adjective 'holy' (qaddishin) is also plural, and Joshua 24:19 uses the same plural adjective with 'God'. Many Christian and Jewish readers have taken the phrase as a half-confession that the king senses the one God. Others note that the speaker is Nebuchadnezzar and hears in Daniel the 'spirit of the gods', as Pharaoh says of Joseph (Genesis 41:38). The Plain follows Nebuchadnezzar's own idiom, 'the holy gods', in 4:8, 9, 18 and 5:11, and 5:14 has 'the gods'.

a: no secret is too much for you
p: The word for 'secret' is borrowed from Persian, one of the loanwords in the debate about the book's date.
b: Raz is a loanword from Old Persian. It is used in chapter 2 for the dream God reveals, and is the root of the later Jewish and Christian use of 'mystery'. The book has a number of Persian loanwords (commentators count about twenty in the Aramaic of chapters 2–7). Those who date the book to the sixth century point out that the Persian empire was already shaping Babylon's court language by the end of the Babylonian period. Critical scholars read them as signs of a Persian-period or later writer. Each side reads the same words its own way.

a: a tree in the middle of the earth
p: A huge tree at the center of the world is a common picture for a great king and his empire.
b: A tree at the center of the earth reaching the sky pictures a world-ruler who shelters all (compare Ezekiel 31:3–14, where Assyria is a cedar whose branches shelter the birds and animals, and where a great fall follows). The birds nesting in the branches and the animals in the shade return in Ezekiel 17:23, where the LORD himself plants a tree for Israel, and in Jesus's parable of the mustard seed (Mark 4:32). Ancient Near Eastern art shows sacred trees at the world's center. The tree is cut down, as the Assyrian cedar was, but a stump stays.

p: 'Watcher' (Aramaic 'ir) occurs only in Daniel 4 in the Bible; here it is a holy angel.
b: Ir is found only in 4:13, 17 and 23. The Old Greek calls the figure 'an angel', Theodotion 'a watcher' (eir, a transliteration). The Aramaic qaddish ('holy one') in the same phrase shows these watchers belong to God's service. In 1 Enoch (a work held as Scripture only by the Ethiopian church), the 'Watchers' are angels who rebel and father the giants (compare Genesis 6:1–4), but in Daniel the term has nothing negative. The Book of Giants and the Genesis Apocryphon, both in Aramaic from Qumran, use the same word for the rebels, so the term was already in Jewish use.

t: The stump that keeps its roots
p: A felled tree with a stump left behind echoes Isaiah's pictures of judgment and hope.
b: Isaiah uses the felling of a great forest for the humbling of Assyria (10:33–34) and then speaks of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1); in Isaiah 6:13 a tenth remains like the stump of a felled oak. Job 14:7–9 hopes that a cut tree will sprout again. In Daniel the stump left in the ground carries the promise that the king's kingdom will be kept for him (4:26). The same picture of judgment that leaves a root is central to the prophets' idea of the remnant.

p: The band may protect the stump, or restrain the king; the text moves from tree to man in the middle of the verse.
b: Verses 15–16 change from 'the stump' to 'him' without warning, which is how the dream turns into the king's own fate. The band of iron and bronze has been read three ways. Some see a metal band around the stump to protect it from splitting, so it can sprout again. Others see fetters on a man gone mad (compare Samson in Judges 16:21 and Zedekiah in 2 Kings 25:7). A third reading takes it as a sign that the king's power would be kept in reserve, bound until the seven periods end. The Old Greek has Nebuchadnezzar handed to prison and bound in chains (Swete 4:14).

p: The Aramaic word 'iddan means a set time; the text never says how long a period was.
b: Iddan is a fixed stretch of time. Whether it means a season, a month or a year is not stated. The Old Greek says 'seven years' (ete). Theodotion keeps the vague 'seven times' (kairoi). Most modern commentators take 'years' as a natural guess, others note that the dream and its history could use a symbolic seven. The same word is used for 'a time, times and half a time' in 7:25, so the Plain does not call the periods in chapter 4 'years'; see the note at 7:25.

t: A decision made in the heavenly court
p: The verdict is announced as the decree of the watchers and holy ones, a picture of God's council.
b: The 'decree of the watchers' and 'word of the holy ones' show the heavenly court at work: God sits as judge, and the council carries out and announces the sentence (compare 1 Kings 22:19–23; Job 1:6; Psalm 82:1; Psalm 89:5–8). The same court reappears in 7:9–10. Some Jewish and Christian readers say the angels simply announce what God has already decided (4:24 calls it 'the decree of the Most High'). Others, noting the plural, see the picture as a real council in which God works with his holy ones. Either way the point is that the sentence is certain, and its aim is stated: 'So all who live will know that the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind.'

a: may the dream belong to those who hate you
p: Daniel wishes the bad news on the king's enemies, a polite way to deliver a hard message.
b: A wish that bad news fall on a king's enemies, not on the king, is a courtly way to deliver a hard message. When the Cushite tells David that Absalom is dead, he says 'May the enemies of my lord the king be like that young man' (2 Samuel 18:32), and Abigail uses a similar wish (1 Samuel 25:26). Daniel is struck silent for an hour because he sees the news is the king's own destruction. He says it plainly in 4:24–25.

p: The Aramaic uses a plural 'they', which can be read as the angels or as the passive.
b: The verbs in 4:25 and 4:32 are third-person plural, 'they will drive you out', 'they will feed you', 'they will drench you'. Aramaic often uses the plural for an unnamed doer, as English uses the passive, and many take it as the watchers of 4:13–17, who carry out the sentence. The Plain uses the passive. Deuteronomy 28:28 lists madness among the covenant curses; Daniel 5:21 later says the same thing happened 'he was driven out from among human beings'.

p: Here 'Heaven' stands for God, a way of speaking that became common in later Jewish writing.
b: Daniel 4:26 is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where 'Heaven' alone is a way of saying God. Later Jewish writing used it constantly: 1 Maccabees (a book Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture) says 'Heaven' where it avoids the word God, and the Mishnah speaks of 'the fear of Heaven'. The same habit lies behind the Gospels: the prodigal son says 'I have sinned against heaven' (Luke 15:18), and Matthew's 'kingdom of heaven' is the same as 'kingdom of God'. The king himself, in 4:34 and 4:37, uses 'heaven' for God as well.

p: The Aramaic tsidqah is 'doing what is right'; the Greek and the Latin turned it into 'alms'.
b: Daniel's advice has two halves: 'doing what is right' (tsidqah) and 'showing mercy to the poor'. Both Greek versions render the verse with 'alms' (eleemosynais): the Old Greek (Swete 4:24) 'redeem all your wrongs with alms', and Theodotion (Swete Dat 4:24) 'redeem your sins with alms and your wrongs with pity for the poor'. Jerome's Latin Vulgate likewise has 'redeem your sins with alms'. See the variant. That wording became a favorite text in Christian teaching on almsgiving; compare Tobit 12:9 (Tobit is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches). Protestant interpreters usually read the Aramaic as a call to turn from sin into just behavior, shown in care for the poor, not as a payment for sin. Jewish usage later made tsedaqah the word for charity.

a: the roof of the royal palace
p: The Aramaic says 'on the palace'; the roof is the usual meaning, but the Old Greek puts him on the city walls.
b: The Aramaic is al heikal malkuta, 'upon the royal palace'. Flat roofs were places to walk in the evening (2 Samuel 11:2, where David sees Bathsheba). Theodotion has 'on the palace'; the Old Greek has him walking 'on the walls of the city and on its towers' (Swete 4:26). Either way the king looks over Babylon. The Plain takes the roof of the royal palace and says so here.

p: Nebuchadnezzar did rebuild Babylon on a huge scale, and his own inscriptions boast of it.
b: Nebuchadnezzar's building program is well known: the Ishtar Gate and Processional Way, the palaces, the city walls, and the great ziggurat. Bricks stamped with his name have been found across the site, and his inscriptions describe his works in first-person boasts that have the same tone as this verse. The words 'Babylon the Great' return in Revelation 14:8 and 18:2, which take over the title for the final, proud world city. His pride matches the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:13–14, who says 'I will ascend to heaven'.

t: The king's madness: what history says
p: No Babylonian text records an illness of Nebuchadnezzar; the best-known parallel is about King Nabonidus.
b: No record from Babylon speaks of Nebuchadnezzar going mad, though the records for his later years are thin. Four explanations are offered. (1) It happened, and was left out of royal inscriptions as embarrassing. A Greek writer, Abydenus, quoted in Eusebius, tells of the king possessed on his palace roof and then vanishing. (2) The story came from Nabonidus (556–539 BC), who spent about ten years at Teima in Arabia; the Prayer of Nabonidus (4Q242, in Aramaic from Qumran) has him struck with a painful ulcer or inflammation for seven years and healed after a Jewish diviner forgave his sin. J. T. Milik first published it in 1956 and Frank Cross studied it in 1984; many see in it a tradition that moved from one king to the other (Collins, Goldingay). (3) A rare mental illness in which people believe they are animals (called boanthropy; R. K. Harrison suggested it). The Plain does not diagnose. (4) A literary picture: the proud king reduced to an animal.

a: his hair grew like an eagle's and his nails like a bird's
p: The Aramaic says 'like eagles' and 'like birds'; English readers often add 'feathers' and 'claws'.
b: The Aramaic compares his hair to 'eagles' and his nails to 'birds', leaving out the word for feathers or claws, so the Plain does the same. The great eagle of Ezekiel 17:3 is the king of Babylon, and Jeremiah 48:40 uses an eagle for the attacker of Moab, whom many read as Babylon. And in Daniel 7:4 the first beast, Babylon, has an eagle's wings that are torn off. The king who imagined himself an eagle over the earth is brought down to the ground, grazing like an ox.

p: He praises the Most High, but the text never says he gave up his own gods.
b: The king raises his eyes to heaven, which is a sign of prayer, and blesses the Most High. Readers have long divided over what this means. Some Jewish and Christian commentators say he became a true worshiper, or at least a God-fearer. Others note that he speaks of 'the King of heaven' and 'the Most High' (not the LORD by name), and the story ends with his glory restored. Naaman, too, confesses the LORD yet asks to keep a place in his master's temple (2 Kings 5:17–18). The text asks for no more than that Nebuchadnezzar learns the one lesson that heaven rules, and that the book's readers hear a pagan king confess it.

p: The stars and the angels are called God's army in the Bible.
b: 'The army of heaven' can mean the angels (1 Kings 22:19; Psalm 103:20–21; Luke 2:13 'the heavenly army') and the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). Other nations worshiped the stars; the Bible says they serve the Most High. Here the point is that God rules above and below: heaven's army and the earth's peoples both serve his purposes.

p: Only Nebuchadnezzar calls God 'King of heaven', and the title joins 'the God of the heavens' used elsewhere.
b: 'King of heaven' is found only here in the Hebrew Bible, a title the king reaches through the story. The Aramaic parts of Ezra use 'the God of the heavens' (Ezra 5:11–12; 6:9–10; the same title as Daniel 2:18–19, 37, 44), and Nehemiah uses it in Hebrew (Nehemiah 1:4–5). In the book it is the language that Jews and non-Jews of the Persian world shared. The chapter ends with Nebuchadnezzar's own judgment: God 'is able to humble' those who walk in pride, which is exactly what he has just learned.

p: Babylonian records show Belshazzar as the crown prince who ran Babylon while his father Nabonidus was in Arabia.
b: Belshazzar (Babylonian Bel-shar-usur) was the eldest son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon (556–539 BC). The Nabonidus Chronicle and a poem called the Verse Account say that Nabonidus spent about ten years at Teima in Arabia and left the army and the kingship in his son's hands, and contracts of the time swear by the lives of both. So a king's son who held power in Babylon, and the 'third' place in the kingdom as the highest on offer (5:7), fits the records. Critics note that Daniel calls him 'king' and the son of Nebuchadnezzar (5:2, 11, 18, 22), and that Greek writers (Herodotus, Xenophon, Berossus) never name him; defenders (Young, Wiseman) answer that he held royal power in fact and that 'son' covers a descendant (see 5:2). Both sides agree the author knew of a Belshazzar who held power.

p: The temple's vessels were carried to Babylon in stages and later returned under Cyrus.
r: 2 Kings 24:13; 2 Kings 25:13–15; 2 Chronicles 36:7, 10, 18; Daniel 1:2; Ezra 1:7–11; Jeremiah 27:16–22
b: Daniel 1:2 says Nebuchadnezzar put the temple's vessels in the treasury of his god's temple. Other texts tell of the removal in 597 and 586 BC, and Jeremiah 27–28 had warned that the rest would follow. Ezra 1:7–11 records Cyrus handing back 5,400 gold and silver vessels. Using them as party cups for gods of metal and stone is the sin of the story: sacred things made common. 1 Maccabees 1:21–24 tells how Antiochus IV took the temple's vessels in 169 BC, a recent memory for readers who date the book to that time.

p: Aramaic 'father' and 'son' can mean ancestor and descendant, or predecessor and successor.
b: Nabonidus, not Nebuchadnezzar, was Belshazzar's father. Defenders of the early date point to wide Semitic use: Jehu is called 'son of Omri' (a king not his father) in an Assyrian inscription, and in the Bible a king's 'son' can be a later heir (Jeremiah 27:7 speaks of Nebuchadnezzar's son and grandson) and Jesus is 'son of David' (Matthew 1:1). Some suggest Nabonidus married a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, which would make Belshazzar a grandson; the sources do not say so. Critical scholars say the author simply thought Belshazzar was Nebuchadnezzar's son. The Plain keeps 'father' and 'son' and lets readers weigh this.

a: sang the praises of their gods, made of gold and silver
p: The five materials echo the Bible's mockery of idols made by hand.
r: Psalm 115:4–8; Psalm 135:15–18; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:3–5; Daniel 5:23; Habakkuk 2:18–19
b: The list 'gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone' comes back, in the same order, in 5:23. Together they carry the Bible's standard argument against idols: gods made by hand cannot see, hear or know (Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10). In the Aramaic section of Daniel the contrast is between these gods and the living God who holds the king's breath (5:23; 6:26).

p: A hand writes on plaster; the Bible elsewhere speaks of the 'finger of God' writing.
orig: פַּס יְדָא (pas yada), 'palm (or extremity) of the hand'
b: Pas yada (here and in 5:24) means the 'palm' or the end of the hand; the exact meaning is uncertain. Only the fingers and hand appear, not a body. The Bible speaks of the 'finger of God' writing the law on stone (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10), and Pharaoh's magicians say 'It is the finger of God' (Exodus 8:19). The writing is on the plaster of the palace wall. The story turns a banquet into a trial, and the law written on stone becomes a verdict written on plaster.

a: rule as third in the kingdom
p: The offer of third place makes sense if Belshazzar was himself second, under Nabonidus.
b: The phrase talti can mean 'third' or 'one of a board of three' (from the word for 'three'; compare the board of three in 6:2). Defenders of the sixth-century date say the offer of 'third' is exactly what we would expect: Nabonidus was first, Belshazzar second, so the highest place left is third. Others take it as a ruling triumvirate. Pharaoh gave Joseph the second place (Genesis 41:40–43) and Mordecai was second to Ahasuerus (Esther 10:3). The Plain keeps 'third' and the reader can weigh the readings.

p: She enters the banquet as someone with authority; the wives are already there, so she is probably the queen mother.
b: The queen speaks after 'the words of the king and his nobles', and she enters the hall though the king's wives are already there (5:2–3). So she is probably not one of his wives but the queen mother, who held great weight at an ancient court (compare Maacah in 1 Kings 15:13 and Nehushta in 2 Kings 24:12). Some identify her with the widow or daughter of Nebuchadnezzar, which fits her knowledge of his time; the sources do not say who she was. The Old Greek calls her 'the queen' as well (Swete 5:9).

a: Daniel, the man the king named Belteshazzar
t: A name given by a king
p: The queen uses the name the king gave Daniel, as a reminder that kings can rename people but not their God.
b: Giving a new name is a sign of control: Pharaoh renamed Joseph (Genesis 41:45), Neco renamed Eliakim 'Jehoiakim' (2 Kings 23:34), and Nebuchadnezzar renamed Mattaniah 'Zedekiah' (2 Kings 24:17). Daniel's Babylonian name is the one used at court (4:8; 5:12), yet the queen says 'Daniel' in 5:12 and the king calls him 'that Daniel' in 5:13. Compare 1:7. The story shows that a king can rename a man but cannot change whom he serves.

p: Daniel is praised for explaining riddles and 'untying knots', meaning to solve hard problems.
orig: אַחֲוָיַת אֲחִידָן וּמְשָׁרֵא קִטְרִין (achavayat achidan umeshare qitrin)
b: Achidan (riddles) matches the Hebrew chidot (Judges 14:12–14; Psalm 78:2). Qitrin means 'knots' and is used here for problems that tie the mind in knots (the word also names 'joints' in 5:6). The phrase may also hint at undoing spells; 5:16 repeats it. The two phrases together say that Daniel's gift was not only dream-reading but solving hard puzzles, which is what the writing is.

a: holds your every breath in his hand
p: Breath and paths belong to God, a thought the Bible repeats for all people.
b: Daniel's charge is that Belshazzar honored lifeless gods and ignored the God who holds his breath. The same idea runs through the Bible: God gives life and takes it back (Genesis 2:7; Job 12:10; 34:14–15; Psalm 104:29), and Paul uses it in Athens (Acts 17:25, 28). The idols 'cannot see, hear or know', while the living God knows all his ways.

a: the writing that was set down
p: The words are weights and also verbs; Daniel reads them as verbs in a prophecy.
orig: מְנֵא מְנֵא תְּקֵל וּפַרְסִין (mene mene teqel ufarsin)
b: The four words are readable Aramaic. Charles Clermont-Ganneau (1886) argued they are weights: a mina (mene), a mina again, a shekel (teqel) and half-minas (parsin), a list of weights. But Daniel hears each word as a verb: mena 'to count', teqal 'to weigh', peras 'to divide', and in 5:28 plays on paras, 'Persia'. The repeated 'mene' is explained in some views as emphasis, in others as an extra coin. The earlier wise men may have read it but could not give it a meaning (5:8). The Old Greek and Theodotion read the words differently from the Aramaic (see the variant).

a: God has counted out your kingdom
p: The three interpretations add 'God has' and 'you have been' to the bare words.
b: Each interpretation takes the word as a verb in a short sentence: counted and finished, weighed and found lacking, split and given. In Aramaic the noun mene sounds like the verb 'counted'. The same word-play, a noun read as a verb, is a classic way of making a message from a short phrase, as Jeremiah does with 'almond' (shaqed) and 'watching' (shoqed) in Jeremiah 1:11–12. The Plain does not add 'the days of'.

p: Egypt pictured the dead weighed against a feather; the Bible's weighing is about a king's character.
b: The Bible often says God weighs people or their hearts (Job 31:6; Proverbs 16:2; 21:2; 1 Samuel 2:3). In Egyptian pictures of judgment after death the dead person's heart is weighed against a feather. A link to Daniel is unlikely, since the image of scales is common everywhere. In Daniel the scales are those of a banquet-hall verdict on a living king, not a rite of the afterlife.

p: The singular peres means 'divided' and sounds like the word for Persians.
b: In the writing the word is parsin (plural, with 'and'); Daniel reads the singular peres, 'divided'. That form sounds like paras, 'Persia'. So one word gives two truths: the kingdom is cut in two, and it goes to the Medes and Persians. This is why the Plain keeps the Aramaic words in the verse and spells out the sense. The Medes come first in 'the Medes and Persians' (5:28; 6:8, 12, 15), the opposite of the order in Esther 1:19.

a: That same night Belshazzar, the Chaldean king, was killed
p: Babylon fell to Cyrus in October 539 BC; Greek writers tell of a banquet night and a king killed.
b: The Nabonidus Chronicle says Cyrus's army defeated the Babylonians at Opis, took Sippar, and that Ugbaru, governor of Gutium, entered Babylon without a battle on 16 Tashritu (about 12 October 539 BC); Cyrus himself came in on the third of Arahsamnu. The Chronicle does not say Belshazzar died. Herodotus (1.191) says Babylon fell while its people were dancing at a festival, and Xenophon (Cyropaedia 7.5) says that during a banquet night the king was killed. Isaiah 21:5 and Jeremiah 51:39, 57 describe a feast and a drunken sleep. Daniel's account matches these. Whether Belshazzar's death is history or tradition, the sources do not settle.

p: No source outside Daniel names a king 'Darius the Mede'; four main answers have been offered.
r: Daniel 6:1, 28; Daniel 9:1; Daniel 11:1; Ezra 4:5; Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28
b: The name 'Darius the Mede' occurs only in Daniel (5:31; 6:1; 9:1; 11:1). The chief answers: (1) Gubaru, the governor of Babylon under Cyrus in the Nabonidus Chronicle (J. C. Whitcomb). Whitcomb keeps Gubaru apart from Ugbaru, the general who took the city and, according to the Chronicle, died soon after, and identifies Darius with Gubaru; Beaulieu and others take Ugbaru and Gubaru to be one man; (2) Cyrus himself, the 'and' in 6:28 meaning 'that is' (D. J. Wiseman); (3) Cyaxares or Astyages, the Median kings; (4) no real person, but a figure drawn from Darius I of Persia (522–486 BC) and from the idea of a Median kingdom between Babylon and Persia (H. H. Rowley; Collins). Each view has gaps: no text gives Gubaru the title 'king', Cyrus was Persian, and Darius I came later. The Plain gives no verdict.

p: English 5:31 is the first verse of Aramaic chapter 6.
b: In the Hebrew Bible, English 5:31 is 6:1, and English 6:1–28 is Aramaic 6:2–29. This site uses the English numbers. 'Received the kingdom' uses the verb qabbel, 'to receive', with no sign that Darius took it by force. Some scholars say it hints that someone else, Cyrus, handed him authority; others say it just means that he took it over.

p: English 6:1 is Aramaic 6:2; the English chapter runs 6:1–28 where the Hebrew Bible has 6:2–29.
b: The verse numbers in this chapter differ: English 5:31 is Aramaic 6:1, and English 6:1–28 is Aramaic 6:2–29. This site uses the English numbers throughout. Note also that the story of the lions' den is set under 'Darius the Mede' (see the note at 5:31).

p: 'Satrap' is a Persian word; Persian satrapies were fewer than 120, and the Old Greek says 127.
b: Achashdarpan is Old Persian xshathrapavan, 'protector of the kingdom'. Satraps governed the great provinces of the Persian empire; Herodotus (3.89) says Darius I set up twenty. Esther 1:1 has 127 'provinces', the number the Old Greek gives for the satraps here. A figure of 120 may be a round number or count smaller districts. Defenders of the early date say the title and office fit the empire that Cyrus founded. Critics say the picture reads like the later Persian system as remembered by a writer far from those years.

p: The plot works because Daniel's God has a 'law' (dat) that can be set against the king's.
b: Dat is a Persian loanword, the word used for the king's decree and also for 'the law of your God' in Ezra 7:12–26 and Esther 3:8, where Haman complains that the Jews' laws differ from the king's. The enemies know that Daniel's faithfulness to the God of his fathers is the one place where he and the king's decrees could collide. The story of the three friends (chapter 3) and Esther use the same pattern, and Hebrews 11:33–34 counts such deliverances among acts of faith.

p: No known Persian king banned prayer to other gods; the ban looks like a trap, and like an echo of later persecutions.
b: Persian kings were known for tolerating the gods of their subjects (the Cyrus Cylinder says as much, and Ezra 6:3–12 gives the temple a royal grant). No outside text records a month-long ban like this. Defenders note that the trap needs only a flattered king and a short ban. Critics find the ban closer to Antiochus IV's decree against Jewish worship (1 Maccabees 1:41–50; 2 Maccabees 6:1–11) and to the ruler cults of the Greek period. Whatever its setting, the story asks what a person should do when the state orders what God forbids (Acts 4:18–20).

t: A law that cannot be repealed
p: The same idea of unchangeable royal law appears in Esther and in a Greek historian's account of Darius III.
b: Esther 1:19 and 8:8 also say that a decree sealed in the king's name could not be taken back. The Greek historian Diodorus (17.30) tells how Darius III regretted executing a man but could not undo his order. The order 'Medes and Persians' puts Media first, as in 5:28 and 6:12, while Esther has 'Persians and Medes' (Esther 1:19); this suits a story set at the moment between the two empires.

p: Solomon's temple prayer told exiles to pray toward the city and the temple.
b: In his temple prayer Solomon asked God to hear those who pray toward the city and the temple from a land of exile (1 Kings 8:48–49). Daniel does just that, with his upstairs windows open toward a city and temple that had lain in ruins since 586 BC. Later Jews prayed facing Jerusalem, and Christians in the East prayed facing east; the Mishnah (Berakhot 4:5–6) tells people abroad to face the Land and Jerusalem. The open windows make his prayer public enough to be seen, and show that he refuses to hide it.

p: Daniel prays three times a day, as the psalmist does; later Jews and Christians kept the same pattern.
b: Psalm 55:17 speaks of praying 'evening, morning and noon'. Daniel's habit became the model for fixed daily prayer. The Jewish custom of three daily prayers is often traced to the Second Temple period and the times of the daily offerings, and the Didache (8:3, an early Christian church manual) tells believers to say the Lord's Prayer three times a day. The text says he knelt, prayed and 'gave thanks' (the Aramaic verb moda, from the same root as Hebrew modeh), so the prayer is more than a request: it is public thanksgiving.

p: Darius's words can be a hope ('may your God rescue you') or a statement ('he will').
b: The verb is a future or wish form, and Aramaic does not mark the difference. Many versions read it as a wish, 'May your God ... deliver you'. The Plain keeps the plain future and lets the reader hear the mix of doubt and hope in a king who has just lost an argument with his own law. Compare Nebuchadnezzar in 3:15, who asks what god could rescue the three friends, and then in 3:28 blesses the God who did.

t: A stone, a seal and a sealed tomb
p: Sealing the den with the king's ring is how a ruler made an order unchangeable; Matthew tells of a sealed tomb.
b: A signet ring pressed into clay or wax closed a door or document with royal authority (Esther 3:12; 8:8). The seal was meant to prevent the nobles or the king from tampering with the den, so that no one could secretly save or kill Daniel. The Gospels have a similar scene: Pilate's guard seals the stone of Jesus's tomb (Matthew 27:60–66). Christian readers have drawn the parallel between a sealed den and a sealed tomb.

p: The word dachavan appears only here; ancient and modern readers have guessed 'food', 'musicians' and 'concubines'.
b: Dachavan is found nowhere else, so its meaning is a guess. The Old Greek and Theodotion do not help much (Theodotion has 'dishes' and the Vulgate 'meals', so both took it as food; the Old Greek has no matching word); others suggested musical instruments, or women brought to the king. Because it follows 'without food' it most likely means some form of pleasure. The Plain says 'nothing to amuse him'.

p: An angel shuts the lions' mouths; Hebrews 11:33 and 1 Maccabees remember Daniel's rescue.
r: Daniel 3:28; Psalm 34:7; Psalm 91:11–13; Hebrews 11:33; 1 Maccabees 2:60; 2 Timothy 4:17
b: In chapter 3 the king says God sent 'his angel' to the furnace (3:28), and Psalm 91:11–13 promises an angel's protection from lions. The author of Hebrews lists those who 'shut the mouths of lions' among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:33), and 1 Maccabees, in the speech of the dying Mattathias, remembers Daniel's innocence and his rescue from the lions (1 Maccabees 2:60). The innocence Daniel claims is the legal word zakhu, which also has the sense of merit before God.

a: the men who had slandered Daniel
p: The Aramaic idiom 'ate his pieces' means to accuse him maliciously.
b: Akal qartsa, 'to eat the pieces of' someone, is an Aramaic idiom for slandering or denouncing a person; it is used of the Chaldeans in 3:8. The Plain turns the idiom into English. A lion eats pieces too, so the story has the accusers eaten by the animals they meant for Daniel, as Psalm 7:15–16 and Proverbs 26:27 say of a pit digger.

a: they and their sons and their wives
p: Killing the families of the guilty was a Persian practice; the law of Moses forbids it.
b: Herodotus (3.119) reports that Darius I put the children and relatives of a plotting noble to death. Esther 9:13–14 has Haman's ten sons hanged. Israel's law says fathers are not to be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16; 2 Kings 14:5–6), yet Achan's family died with him (Joshua 7:24–25). The story shows a ruthless empire, not the law of God, and readers have always disagreed about whether the author approves.

p: 'The living God' is the Bible's contrast with dead idols; here a foreign king uses it.
r: Joshua 3:10; Jeremiah 10:10; Hosea 1:10; Psalm 42:2; Matthew 16:16; Daniel 6:20
b: Elaha chayya is the Aramaic form of the Hebrew El chay. It sets the God who acts against idols that do nothing (Jeremiah 10:10; Joshua 3:10). Darius's decree has three verbs of action, 'saves, rescues, does signs and wonders', and repeats Nebuchadnezzar's praise in 4:1–3 and 4:34: the same kingdom that 'never will be destroyed'. The book places four royal confessions (2:47; 3:28–29; 4:34–37; 6:25–27) at the ends of the court stories so that the reader sees a pattern.

a: and during the reign of Cyrus
p: The Aramaic 'and' can mean 'even', which would make Darius and Cyrus the same person.
b: The Aramaic u, 'and', may join two reigns or explain the first: 'in the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus the Persian'. D. J. Wiseman proposed the second reading and with it that Darius the Mede was Cyrus under a different name (he points to 1 Chronicles 5:26, where 'and' also seems to explain). Others read two reigns, one after the other. The Old Greek says Cyrus 'took over his kingdom' (Swete 6:28), and Daniel's later visions are dated by Cyrus (10:1).

a: In the first year of Belshazzar
t: Why chapter 7 is dated before chapter 5
p: Chapter 7 is dated to Belshazzar's first year, about 553 BC, earlier than the feast in chapter 5.
b: The vision comes in Belshazzar's first year, about 553 BC if his rule is counted from Nabonidus's departure to Teima (see 5:1), and so before the feast of chapter 5 and the fall of Babylon in 539. Readers who take the book as the work of the sixth century say that the editor put the court stories (1–6) before the visions (7–12) by subject, not by date. Critical scholars add that chapters 2 to 7 are built as a chiasm in Aramaic (A 2 and 7: four kingdoms; B 3 and 6: deliverance from death; C 4 and 5: proud kings humbled), so the order is literary. Papyrus 967 of the Old Greek, as its editors report, puts chapters 7–8 before 5–6, so the Greek book is arranged differently from the Aramaic one.

a: told the main points of it
p: The Aramaic says he told the 'head' of the matters, the summary; the rest is in the angel's explanation.
b: Resh millin, 'the head (sum or start) of the matters', means either a summary or the beginning. It marks the shift in the book from stories told about Daniel to a vision told by Daniel in his own voice ('I, Daniel', 7:15). The verse is also the bridge: Daniel 'wrote' the dream, which prepares for the command to seal the book in 12:4.

p: Winds from every direction stir the sea; God's winds scatter and gather nations in the prophets.
r: Jeremiah 49:36; Zechariah 2:6; Zechariah 6:5; Ezekiel 37:9; Daniel 8:8; Daniel 11:4
b: 'The four winds' are the four directions, and they come from heaven, so the unrest on the sea is under God's hand. Jeremiah 49:36 and Zechariah 6:5 also tie the winds to God's actions among the nations. Daniel 8:8 and 11:4 use the same four winds for the breakup of Alexander's empire. The Old Greek has the winds 'fall' on the sea (Swete 7:2).

p: In the ancient Near East the sea is chaos; Canaanite myth had a sea-god defeated by a cloud-rider.
r: Genesis 1:2; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 89:9–10; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9–10; Revelation 13:1
b: In Genesis 1:2 and the Psalms the sea is the enemy of order, home of monsters that God subdues (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9–10). The best-known pre-Israelite parallel is the Ugaritic story where Baal, 'rider of the clouds', defeats Yam, 'Prince Sea'. Scholars such as J. A. Emerton and Collins see Daniel 7 using that old pattern: beasts from the sea, a court, and a figure on the clouds. Whether Daniel borrowed directly from Canaanite stories or from Israel's own version of the pattern is disputed. Revelation 13:1 makes the sea the source of its beast.

p: The prophets already picture hostile nations as wild beasts; four is the number for the whole world.
r: Hosea 13:7–8; Jeremiah 5:6; Ezekiel 29:3; Ezekiel 32:2; Daniel 8:3–8; Revelation 13:1–2
b: Hosea 13:7–8 has the LORD as a lion, leopard and bear, and Jeremiah 5:6 has a lion, wolf and leopard attacking Judah. Ezekiel calls Pharaoh a great sea monster (29:3; 32:2). Here the beasts are the empires. Four is the number of the world's corners (see 'the four winds'), and four-empire schemes are known outside the Bible too (see 7:17). The Plain uses the word 'beasts', as in Revelation 13, which gathers all four animals into one beast.

a: looked like a lion, but it had an eagle's wings
p: All the standard readings take the winged lion as Babylon; it matches Jeremiah's lion and Babylonian art.
r: Jeremiah 4:7; Jeremiah 49:19–22; Jeremiah 48:40; Ezekiel 17:3; Lamentations 4:19; Daniel 4:33
b: Jeremiah 4:7 sends a lion, 'a destroyer of nations', from the north, and Jeremiah 48:40 and 49:19–22 use an eagle and a lion against Moab and Edom; many read all these as Babylon, and Ezekiel 17:3 names the eagle as Babylon's king. Striding lions in glazed brick line Babylon's Processional Way (the lion was the animal of the goddess Ishtar); winged lions are better known from Assyrian and Persian art. Rashi says plainly that the first beast 'is the kingdom of Babylon', as Jeremiah also saw it (Rashi on 7:4). All the standard readings, ancient and modern, agree that the first beast is Babylon. Both Greek versions, as Swete prints them, call it a 'lioness', and Revelation 13:2 gives the beast a lion's mouth.

a: it was given a human heart
t: The lion that learned it was human
p: The first beast is made to stand like a human and given a human heart, as Nebuchadnezzar's story ends.
b: Stripped of its wings, the lion is lifted up, stands on two feet, and receives a human heart. This looks back to chapter 4: the king's heart was taken from him and given to an animal (4:16), and when he lifted his eyes his reason returned (4:34, 36). In Psalm 9:20 the nations learn they are 'only human'. The pattern is that a kingdom is human when it knows it is under God. Compare the spec note at 7:8.

t: The second beast: Media or Persia?
p: The bear is Media in some readings and Persia in others; the three ribs are read at least three ways.
b: In the scheme Babylon–Media–Persia–Greece the bear is Media (Collins; Rowley). Leviticus Rabbah 13:5 also takes the bear as Media, but in a third scheme of its own (Babylon, Media, Greece, Edom; see the note at 7:17). In the scheme Babylon–Persia–Greece–Rome it is the Medo-Persian empire, 'raised on one side' because Persia outweighed Media (Jerome). Rashi names Persia and gives two readings of the ribs: provinces forever rebelling and being re-swallowed, or three Persian kings, Cyrus, Ahasuerus and Darius. Others take the ribs as three conquests (Lydia, Babylon, Egypt). Many critical scholars say the ribs cannot be fixed.

p: The leopard with four wings and four heads is Greece in one scheme and Persia in the other.
b: In the scheme Babylon–Media–Persia–Greece the leopard is Persia, with four heads for four Persian kings or four regions. In the scheme Babylon–Medo-Persia–Greece–Rome it is Greece, as Rashi says, and the four heads are the four generals among whom Alexander's empire was divided (compare 8:8, 22; 11:4), the four wings the speed of his conquests. The leopard of Hosea 13:7 and Jeremiah 5:6 sits crouching by a path.

t: The fourth beast and Revelation's beast
p: Revelation gathers all four of Daniel's animals and the ten horns into a single beast from the sea.
b: The fourth beast has no animal likeness, only iron teeth and ten horns. It matches the iron legs of the statue in Daniel 2:40–43. Revelation 13:1 sees 'a beast coming up out of the sea, with ten horns and seven heads', and Revelation 13:2 says 'The beast I saw was like a leopard. Its feet were like a bear's, and its mouth was like a lion's mouth.' Revelation 17:12 explains the ten horns as ten kings. John thus folds all of Daniel's beasts into one final power.

p: A small horn uproots three others; its identity is explained at 7:24–25.
b: The little horn is the book's most disputed figure. The views, covered at 7:24–25, are: Antiochus IV Epiphanes (c. 175–164 BC) in the critical majority and in many conservative scholars; Titus or Rome's rulers (Rashi); the Antichrist, a future ruler (Hippolytus, Jerome and the Dispensational tradition); the papacy in the Protestant historicist tradition. The horn is small at first and then 'looked greater than the ones beside it' (7:20).

t: Spec: how human is each beast?
p: Claude's theory: chapters 4 and 7 measure each power by whether it admits it is only human.
b: Claude's theory (spec). Chapter 4 teaches that a king stops being human when he forgets that heaven rules, and recovers his humanity only when he looks up (4:34). Chapter 7 repeats the lesson in animals: the first beast is given a human heart and stands on two feet (7:4); the fourth beast's horn has human eyes and a mouth that boasts (7:8), a human look without a human heart, and never learns; the last figure comes 'like a son of man' (7:13) and is the one who truly bears the human name. On this reading 'human' is the chapter's measure: those who accept being creatures are given a kingdom. The link from 7:4 to chapter 4 is well known (Collins and others note it); the pattern as a whole across the three beasts and the horn is my own suggestion, and I have not found it argued this way.

p: The plural 'thrones' was read as seats for angelic judges, for God and the Messiah, or for judging the nations and charity toward Israel.
b: Daniel gives only the plural 'thrones'. Most commentators see seats for the heavenly court who sit with God (7:10; compare Revelation 4:4; 20:4). Rabbi Akiva said one throne was for God and one for David, that is, the Messiah, and Rabbi Yose answered that he was profaning the divine presence (Hagigah 14a, which names him Yose the Galilean; Sanhedrin 38b, which says only Rabbi Yose). Rashi says one throne is for judging the nations and the other for charity toward Israel. Christian readers have found in the second throne the Son at the Father's right hand (Psalm 110:1; Mark 14:62).

p: The Aramaic 'attiq yomin means an old man; the title appears only in this chapter.
orig: עַתִּיק יוֹמִין (attiq yomin), 'one advanced in days'
b: Attiq yomin is found only in 7:9, 13 and 22. It pictures God as an old, wise judge, white-haired and long-lived, and God's age as the sign of his authority. The Canaanite god El is called 'father of years' and is pictured as wise and gray-bearded, a parallel that Emerton, Day and others propose as the source of the picture. 1 Enoch 46:1 (a work held as Scripture by the Ethiopian church) has 'one who had a head of days' beside a son of man. The Plain keeps the title 'the Ancient of Days'. Revelation 1:14 gives Christ the Ancient of Days's white hair, a sign some Christian readers have taken to mean that Christ shares the Father's identity.

a: fire kept burning in its wheels
p: The wheeled throne of fire recalls Ezekiel's chariot-throne and Enoch's vision.
b: Ezekiel saw wheels beside the living creatures and a throne above (Ezekiel 1:15–28; 10:2). Daniel's fiery throne with wheels uses that picture, and 1 Enoch 14:18–22 (a work held as Scripture by the Ethiopian church) tells of a throne with wheels like the sun and a stream of fire. Jewish mystical writing later built the 'chariot' tradition on these passages. The Aramaic galgilohi, 'its wheels', comes from the same root as galgal, the Hebrew word Ezekiel uses (10:2, 6).

p: Fire flows from the throne as it does from God in Psalms and Isaiah; it will judge the beast.
b: Fire accompanies God's appearing (Psalm 50:3; 97:3; Isaiah 66:15). Here a stream pours from before him, to burn the beast (7:11). The river in Revelation 22:1 flows with the water of life from God's throne, the opposite image. In 1 Enoch 14:19 (a work held as Scripture by the Ethiopian church) a river of fire also flows from beneath the throne. The picture is of a holiness that burns what opposes it.

a: tens of thousands of tens of thousands
p: Revelation 5:11 borrows this crowd of servants around the throne.
b: Each Aramaic pair, 'a thousand of thousands' and 'a myriad of myriads' (the Plain: 'thousands upon thousands' and 'tens of thousands of tens of thousands'), means a number too large to count. Revelation 5:11 uses the same words for the angels around the throne: 'ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands times thousands'. Deuteronomy 33:2 and Psalm 68:17 also picture God surrounded by crowds of holy ones. The court is large and the verdict will not be hidden.

p: Heaven keeps records of deeds; Revelation 20:12 uses the same scene for the last judgment.
b: The Bible knows a book of life (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1) and a book of remembrance (Malachi 3:16). Daniel's 'books' are records of deeds. Revelation 20:12 says 'books were opened', and then names another book, the book of life. In 1 Enoch (a work held as Scripture by the Ethiopian church) heaven's records are also read at the judgment. The court sits to give a verdict, not only to hear the horn's words.

p: The first three beasts lose their power but not their existence: peoples outlast the empires that ruled them.
orig: זְמַן וְעִדָּן (zeman ve-iddan), 'a season and a time'
b: The first three beasts lose their rule at the court's verdict, while the fourth is killed. Their life is 'prolonged' for a season and a time. In critical readings this means the Babylonian, Median and Persian peoples live on under the Greek empire, as their cultures did. In Rome-as-fourth readings it means the earlier empires' peoples continue inside the fourth. The words are zeman and iddan, the same time-words as in 2:21 ('he changes times and seasons') and a short form of the periods in 7:25.

t: How the New Testament uses this verse
p: Jesus and the New Testament writers quote the figure on the clouds again and again.
r: Mark 13:26; Mark 14:62; Matthew 24:30; Matthew 26:64; Luke 21:27; Acts 7:56; Revelation 1:7
b: Jesus joins Daniel 7:13 with Psalm 110:1 before the high priest: 'you will see the Son of Man sitting at the Power's right hand and coming on the clouds of the sky' (Matthew 26:64; compare Mark 14:62). He speaks of the Son of Man coming on the clouds in the Olivet discourse (Mark 13:26; Matthew 24:30; Luke 21:27). Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand (Acts 7:56), and Revelation 1:7 joins the coming on the clouds with Zechariah 12:10. In Daniel the movement is toward the Ancient of Days, to be given a kingdom. In the Gospels it is often read as a coming to earth or as vindication of Jesus. The Greek preposition differs among the witnesses. Swete's Old Greek of Daniel 7:13 has the figure coming 'on the clouds' (epi ton nephelon), while Theodotion (Swete Dat 7:13) and the Aramaic have 'with' (meta). Matthew 26:64 has epi and Mark 14:62 has meta; whether this shows which Greek form each Gospel knew is debated, and the variant at 7:13 sets out the readings. How the New Testament moves from Daniel's picture to the Gospels' is a topic of its own (see the topic page on the Son of Man).

p: In the Old Testament the one who rides on clouds is the LORD himself.
b: In the Old Testament, clouds are God's vehicle: he 'rides on the clouds' (Psalm 68:4; Isaiah 19:1; Psalm 104:3). In the Ugaritic texts Baal bears the title 'rider of the clouds'. A human figure who comes with the clouds is therefore given something that elsewhere belongs only to God. Some conclude from this that the figure shares divine glory (Boyarin); others, that the image only shows that his kingdom comes from heaven, in contrast to the beasts from the sea (Collins, Goldingay).

a: one like a son of man
t: 'Like a human being': description or title?
p: The Aramaic means 'like a human being'; whether it is already a title is debated.
orig: כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ (kevar enash), 'like a son of man'
r: Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1; Daniel 8:17; Revelation 1:13; Revelation 14:14; Mark 14:62
b: Bar enash is an ordinary Aramaic phrase for a human (Hebrew ben adam, used of Ezekiel about ninety times and in Psalm 8:4). The Aramaic here has 'like' (ke): the figure looks like a person, in contrast to the beasts. A common scholarly view (Casey, Dunn) takes the phrase as a description, not yet the title 'the Son of Man', which then grows from this verse in the Gospels, or from the Similitudes of 1 Enoch (46–71) and 4 Ezra 13, or from the plain idiom. Christian tradition from Mark 14:62 and Revelation 1:13 reads the figure in Daniel as already the Messiah, and Boyarin argues that Daniel's figure is already a second divine figure, so that the title was not new with the Gospels. The Plain keeps lower case, as in Revelation 1:13 and 14:14 on this site, and the Daniel 8:17 phrase 'son of man' uses the same Hebrew idiom for a human being.

a: He came to the Ancient of Days
p: The Old Greek says the figure appeared 'as the Ancient of Days', not that he came to him.
b: The Hebrew-Aramaic text, supported by Theodotion, has the figure come 'to' the Ancient of Days and be brought near. The Old Greek reads 'as an ancient of days he was present' (hos palaios hemeron), which makes the two figures one. The Old Greek reading seems to come from a different underlying text or a rereading; scholars disagree on whether it is a mistake (Ziegler's edition, following Montgomery, treats it as a corruption of heos tou palaiou, 'to the ancient one') or a deliberate view that the figure is likened to God (Lust; Reynolds, Biblica 89, 2008). See the variant for the witnesses.

t: Who is the one like a son of man?
p: Readers have seen the Messiah, an angel, a divine figure, or the faithful people of Israel.
r: Daniel 7:18, 22, 27; Daniel 12:1; 1 Enoch 46:1–4; 4 Ezra 13:3; Psalm 110:1; Mark 14:62
b: (1) The Messiah: Rashi ('That is the King Messiah'); the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a: with the clouds if Israel is worthy, poor on a donkey if not); 1 Enoch 46–71 and 4 Ezra 13 picture such a figure, though the date of the Enoch section is disputed. (2) An angel, most often Michael (Collins; the NABRE note lists him), the heavenly patron of Israel (10:21; 12:1); Gabriel (8:16; 9:21) has also been proposed. (3) A divine second figure beside the Ancient of Days (Boyarin). (4) A symbol of the holy ones of 7:18, 22 and 27: the faithful people of Israel (Noth; Casey; Dunn; N. T. Wright, who adds that Jesus saw himself as their representative) or their angels. Rashi himself takes the holy ones of 7:25 to be Israel. (5) Jesus, in the Christian tradition from Mark 14:62 on: the Messiah reading (1) applied to him, often joined with (3). Several overlap; the chapter itself explains the vision only through the 'holy ones'.

p: The Aramaic verb is the one used for serving God and the gods in the rest of the book.
b: The verb pelach is used for serving the king's gods and God (3:12, 14, 17–18, 28; 6:16, 20). The Old Greek renders it latreuousa (cult service), and Theodotion douleuousin (they serve). All peoples serving a figure with an everlasting kingdom is therefore either a royal service or a sign of worship. Some take it as the service owed to a king; others see in it a sign of divine honor, and many Christian readers see the honor due to the Son. The Qumran text 4Q246 (a fragment in Aramaic) says someone 'will be called Son of God and they will call him Son of the Most High', whose kingdom is everlasting, and its identity is also debated.

t: The kingdom that does not pass away
p: The kingdom promised to David and the kingdom of Daniel 2:44 meet in this verse.
r: 2 Samuel 7:13, 16; Daniel 2:44; Daniel 4:3; Daniel 6:26; Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15
b: The language of a kingdom that does not pass away comes from God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:13, 16) and returns across the book: the stone becomes a mountain (2:44), Nebuchadnezzar and Darius praise the same kingdom (4:3; 6:26), and here it is given to the figure and, in 7:18 and 27, to the holy ones. Gabriel's promise to Mary draws on it (Luke 1:33), and Revelation 11:15 announces it.

p: A rare Aramaic word, nidneh, means a sheath: the body holds the spirit as a scabbard holds a sword.
b: Nidneh occurs only here in the Aramaic of the Bible and once in Hebrew (1 Chronicles 21:27, of a sword's sheath). Here it is a picture of the body as the scabbard of the spirit. The Plain adds 'of my body' to make the picture clear; the Aramaic says 'in the sheath'. The Old Greek has no such image. The same trembling shows up in 8:27 and 10:8, 16.

p: From here on Daniel needs an angel to interpret; this is a mark of apocalyptic writing.
r: Daniel 8:15–16; Daniel 9:21–22; Zechariah 1:9; Ezekiel 40:3–4; Revelation 17:1; 1 Enoch 21:5
b: In chapters 2 and 4 Daniel is the interpreter, with God's help. In chapter 7 he becomes the one who needs an interpreter, and an angel supplies it, as in Zechariah 1:9 and Ezekiel 40:3–4. Scholars call this the 'interpreting angel' and take it as a mark of the apocalypse as a kind of writing (see the topic on apocalyptic literature): the vision is heavenly, closed to human wisdom, and understood only by revelation. The figures standing by are the court of 7:10.

p: Three schemes: Media separate, Medo-Persia joined, or the rabbinic Babylon-Media-Greece-Edom.
b: (A) Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece: Collins, Rowley, Hartman and Di Lella and most critical scholars. The author counts a separate Median kingdom (Darius the Mede, 5:31; 6:1), following Isaiah 13:17 and Jeremiah 51:11, 28. The fourth kingdom is Alexander's and its Seleucid heirs, and the little horn is Antiochus IV. (B) Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome: Hippolytus, Jerome, Rashi (on 7:4–7, with Titus as the last king on 7:24), most Christian interpreters including Calvin. (C) A rabbinic scheme of its own: Leviticus Rabbah 13:5, reading Daniel 7, takes the lion as Babylon, the bear as Media (Rabbi Yohanan's reading of the word), the leopard as Greece and the fourth beast as Edom, that is Rome; it has no Persia. Genesis Rabbah 2:4 reads Genesis 1:2 in the same way (tohu is Babylon, bohu Media, darkness Greece, the deep the wicked kingdom, Edom) and does not cite Daniel 7 in its body text. Neither midrash is scheme (A) or (B). Greek and Latin writers also counted empires in fours, Aemilius Sura (in Velleius Paterculus 1.6.6) giving Assyria, Media, Persia and Macedonia, and the Sibylline Oracles (book 4) do much the same. See the topic on the four kingdoms, and chapter 2.

a: the holy ones of the Most High
p: Angels or the faithful of Israel? Scholars defend both readings, and some combine them.
orig: קַדִּישֵׁי עֶלְיוֹנִין (qaddishe elyonin), 'holy ones of the Most High'
b: Two readings. (1) Angels: 'holy ones' means heavenly beings elsewhere (4:13, 17; 8:13; Deuteronomy 33:2; Job 5:1) and at Qumran (the War Scroll); the vision is then of heaven's victory, with Israel its beneficiary (Collins). (2) The faithful Jews who are persecuted: they are the ones the horn wears down (7:21, 25); 7:27 says the kingdom is given to 'the people of the holy ones'; 8:24 and 12:7 call Israel a 'people of holy ones' or 'holy people'. Some combine them: the angels and the people stand or fall together (Goldingay). The final 'Most High' is plural (elyonin) as a plural of majesty. Revelation calls the persecuted 'the saints' (Revelation 13:7), whose site term is not the one used here.

a: made war on the holy ones
p: In the critical reading this is Antiochus IV's attack on Jewish worship in 167–164 BC.
b: Critical readers see here the persecution described in 1 Maccabees 1:41–64 and 2 Maccabees 6–7: the temple profaned in December 167 BC, the Sabbath and circumcision banned, copies of the law burned, and faithful Jews killed. Readers who date the book early (and futurist readers) apply it to a coming ruler. For Christian readers Revelation 13:7 reuses this verse of the beast.

p: The Aramaic 'judgment was given to the holy ones' can mean a verdict in their favor or authority to judge.
b: The phrase dina yehav le- means 'judgment was given for' or 'to' the holy ones. Some take it as a verdict in their favor, setting the wrongs against them right (Collins, Goldingay; the NIV and other versions take this side). The Plain's 'went to' leaves both readings open. Others take it as the right to sit in judgment, as in 1 Corinthians 6:2 ('the saints will judge the world') and Revelation 20:4. The Greek 'to the holy ones' fits either.

a: a fourth kingdom that will be on the earth
t: The fourth kingdom and its ten kings
p: The fourth beast is Greece and the Seleucids in one reading and Rome in the other; the ten horns follow.
b: (1) Greece: the critical view (Porphyry, whose objections Jerome answers; Collins; Goldingay). The ten horns are ten kings of the Greek-Seleucid line (the lists differ), and the 'other' horn is Antiochus IV, said to have removed three rivals when he took the throne in 175 BC. (2) Rome: Hippolytus, Irenaeus, Jerome, Calvin and Isaac Newton. For Hippolytus and Irenaeus the ten horns are ten kingdoms into which the Roman empire will divide before the Antichrist; for historicists they are the kingdoms of Europe after Rome's fall. (3) Rashi, on 7:24, says that the last king who rises after the ten is Titus, which places the fourth kingdom in Rome. The horn's identity is discussed at 7:24–25.

a: ten kings will stand up from this kingdom
p: Antiochus IV, Titus, a Roman emperor, the pope, the Turk or a future Antichrist: the views and who holds them.
r: Daniel 7:8, 20–21, 25; Daniel 8:9–12, 23–25; Daniel 9:26–27; Daniel 11:21–45; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Revelation 13:5–8
b: (1) Antiochus IV Epiphanes: the critical majority (Collins, Hartman and Di Lella) and many conservative scholars for chapter 8. 'Speaking against the Most High' and 'changing the times and the law' fit his decrees (1 Maccabees 1:41–50). (2) Titus, the Roman destroyer of the temple: Rashi on 7:8. (3) A future Antichrist: Hippolytus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Jerome, Catholic futurists such as Ribera and Bellarmine, and Dispensationalists (Pentecost). (4) The papacy: Protestant historicists from the Reformation, including Newton, and Adventists (Uriah Smith). The Westminster Confession 25.6 calls the pope 'that Antichrist' without naming Daniel 7. The Reformers did not agree on the horn: Luther's Preface to Daniel, as described in studies of his eschatology, reads the fourth beast as Rome and the little horn of chapter 7 as the Turk (Mohammed's kingdom), while he names the pope as Antichrist elsewhere. (5) A Roman emperor or Roman power in the first century: preterists (the Catholic Alcazar, and Moses Stuart). Several hold double fulfillment: Antiochus now and a final ruler later (compare 8:23–25 and 11:36–45 in the neighboring parts).

p: Pride that speaks against God is the sign of the tyrant in Isaiah, Daniel, Paul and Revelation.
b: The horn's 'big words' (7:8, 20) are now named: they are spoken against God. The pattern goes back to the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:13–14 ('I will make myself like the Most High') and forward to the 'man of lawlessness' in 2 Thessalonians 2:4 and the beast in Revelation 13:5–6. For critical readers it fits Antiochus's title Epiphanes, 'God made manifest', which his coins carry.

a: change the appointed times and the law
p: Antiochus's decrees banned the Sabbath, the festivals and circumcision.
b: Aramaic zimnin are fixed times: festivals and the calendar. Dat is the law. 1 Maccabees 1:41–50 and 2 Maccabees 6:6 report that Antiochus forbade the Sabbath and feasts, circumcision and the offerings, and 1 Maccabees 1:54 dates the 'abomination' to 15 Kislev 167 BC. Some scholars see the 'times' as a reference to the calendar in particular. For other readers it refers to any tyrant's attack on God's law.

a: a time, times and half a time
t: A time, times and half a time
p: Three and a half periods: 3½ years of persecution, a broken seven, 1,260 years or a future tribulation.
orig: עִדָּן וְעִדָּנִין וּפְלַג עִדָּן (iddan veiddanin ufelag iddan)
r: Daniel 4:16; Daniel 8:14; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 12:7, 11–12; Revelation 11:2–3; Revelation 12:6, 14; Revelation 13:5
b: Iddan is a 'period' (see 4:16); iddanin is plural or dual, so the total is 1 + 2 + ½ = 3½ periods. Views: (1) three and a half years, half of a 'seven' (compare 9:27); in the critical reading from the end of 167 to the end of 164 BC, a little over three years (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52); (2) a symbolic 'broken' seven, a limited time of trouble; (3) 1,260 years, by the day-for-a-year principle used by historicists; (4) a future tribulation of 3½ years (Dispensationalists). Revelation uses it as 'time, times and half a time' (12:14), 42 months (13:5) and 1,260 days (12:6). Rashi calls the end 'obscure'. See the topic Three and a Half Years.

a: His kingdom is a kingdom that lasts forever
p: 'His' can mean the Most High's, the one like a son of man's, or the people's; the variant is about the people.
b: The Aramaic has 'his kingdom', with no clear subject. It may refer to the Most High (the nearest named person), to the one like a son of man (7:14), or to the people of the holy ones. The three views of 7:13 fit the three readings. The Greek witnesses also differ on 'the people' (see the variant). In Revelation the saints 'rule on the earth' (Revelation 5:10) and 'will reign forever' (22:5).

a: This is where the account ends
p: The Aramaic stops at 7:28; the Hebrew resumes at 8:1.
b: The Aramaic that began at 2:4 ends here. Chapters 8–12 return to Hebrew. Daniel keeps the matter 'in my heart', as Jacob did with Joseph's dreams (Genesis 37:11) and as Mary does in Luke 2:19, 51. No one has settled why the book changes language twice; the main proposals are that the Aramaic part was written for readers of the common language of the empire, that the chiasm 2–7 was kept as one unit, or that the book was put together from two works. The note at 2:4 has the details.
